title: 'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil
description: Northern Ireland defenders Nat Johnson and Rebecca Holloway tell BBC Sport NI of their dream of reaching a first ever Women's World Cup as NI go through the play-offs.
fullText:
A World Cup staged in Brazil is the stuff of dreams for any footballer and the chance to experience that is on offer for Northern Ireland as they begin their play-off journey against Portugal with hope of securing a spot at next year's tournament.

It will be a difficult ask for Michael McArdle's side, which has been hit by a spate of injuries and features five new faces, but there is a quiet confidence in the group before what will be, for some of them, the biggest games in their careers to date.

First up, in what is set to be an arduous journey in search of a World Cup debut, is Friday's home leg at Inver Park (19:30 BST) against the Portuguese.

"When you're growing up, Brazil is the place to be, it's the home of football. It really doesn't get much better than that," said Norwich City defender Natalie Johnson.

"The fact that we are at this point and that it could be a reality, you don't need much more motivation than that.

"There's a lot on the line, but we are taking it one game at a time and I think if you look at it that way, nothing is impossible. Obviously there is that dream at the end of it, but we're focused on the game in front of us."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

As one of the lowest-ranked European sides in the play-offs, it is a difficult route to next summer's tournament for Northern Ireland.

If they overcome Portugal they will then face Croatia or Iceland in the next round. If they make it through those games, they will likely have an inter-continental play-off to make it the whole way to Brazil.

Portugal inflicted two defeats on in NI in Euro 2025 qualifying and sit 28 places higher in the Fifa world rankings, but Johnson and her side are not daunted by the task in front of them and instead want to embrace it.

"We absolutely believe these games are winnable," she added.

"We have a lot of experience in this team and the young players coming in bring their own individual experience and they really add to the squad. It's a good balance and we are going in to get something out of this.

"Any Portugal side is going to be very technical and we're expecting a very fast-paced game. We're going to have to be at our best to face that, quick football, and that's what we're working towards.

"On paper it might look like there is a big gap between the teams, but at the end of the day, it is a game of football and I think particularly on our home pitch it will be a much more level playing field."

Birmingham City defender Rebecca Holloway is one of the few survivors from the squad that qualified for Euro 2022, NI's first major tournament.

There have been a lot of changes to the squad since, but Holloway is excited for the future rather than dwelling on past achievements.

"It feels like a long time ago in a way, especially when you look at how much the squad has changed, but I think that's also what is very exciting," she said.

"It's like a new generation coming through and I think it's also important that we have some experienced players here to help those new faces. We're excited to see what they can do and encourage them to play with confidence and freedom and do what they are good at.

"We're slowly closing the gap on Portugal and the so-called bigger nations. They had a narrow 2-1 win over us at home in 2024 after a 4-0 away defeat, I think that shows that we are getting closer."

McArdle's youthful side do not have far to look for inspiration as to how to punch above their weight.

After assembling in camp on Monday, the team watched Northern Ireland's men's side 0-0 draw with Georgia.

That stalemate ensured Michael O'Neill's side stayed top of their Nations League group after picking up eight points from four games without conceding a goal.

"It was brilliant watching them play with such youth and energy and the exciting football that they are playing.

"This younger generation play with no fear and I think that is what the men's senior team are doing.

"I am hoping the young players see that and we can adopt the same attitude. I think we were all watching thinking we can't wait to do this on Friday."

title: How can home nations reach Women's World Cup?
description: England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland are among those hoping to qualify for next year's Women's World Cup. What awaits them in the play-offs?
fullText:
England must get through two rounds of home and away ties to qualify for the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Sarina Wiegman's European champions will play Greece in Crete in round one of the play-offs, with the first leg on Friday, 9 October at 17:30 BST.

The second leg will be played at home, at King Power Stadium in Leicester, on Tuesday, 13 October at 19:30 BST.

Commentary for both England matches will be on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Should England beat Greece over two games, they will face the winners of Slovakia v Ukraine, with the away fixture played first.

The exact dates of the potential second-leg fixtures are to be confirmed, although they will take place between 26 November and 5 December 2026.

England head coach Wiegman named her initial squad last month, with Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly notable absentees.

When asked why they were left out, Wiegman said: "They have not been playing to their full potential.

"Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us."

Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "That is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and, of course, they want to work on that."

All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup

Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are also involved in the play-offs as they chase World Cup places.

As with England, they are in action on Friday.

In round one, Wales face Albania at 17:00 BST - with coverage on BBC Two Wales from 16:45 BST.

Scotland play the Czech Republic at 18:00 BST, available to watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Alba.

Northern Ireland take on Portugal at 19:00 BST, available on BBC iPlayer.

The Republic of Ireland will play Kazakhstan at 12:00 BST.

Despite England securing five wins from their six qualifying matches, world champions Spain finished top of the Lionesses' group and secured the one automatic spot.

Wiegman said: "We knew what the play-offs would look like and, while we're pleased with the draw against Greece, the focus now is on making sure we're really well prepared.

"We want to dominate games and have a lot of the ball and that's something we will prepare for carefully."

England did not want to go through the play-offs but were given an unkind draw in the qualifying groups when they met world champions Spain.

However, Wiegman's side are in a strong position for the play-offs and will fancy their chances against Greece, who sit 55 places beneath them in the Fifa world rankings.

England also beat potential round two opponents Ukraine in both matches in the qualifying group stage, with an aggregate 9-1 score.

Northern Ireland face a tricky tie against a talented young squad from Portugal in round one. Portugal twice beat Northern Ireland in Euro 2025 qualifying.

Their task gets even harder if they make it through to round two, with potential opponents Iceland proving to be difficult to break down in their matches against England this year.

Scotland are hoping to reach just their second Women's World Cup finals, after a 2019 appearance. They failed to qualify in 2023 but have performed well this year, including drawing with Belgium, showing that they can compete with Europe's strongest teams.

They would need to produce their best in round two if they meet big-hitters Sweden, who have been semi-finalists in the past two Women's World Cups.

Wales have never beaten a top-20 ranked nation in a competitive fixture and are likely to need to do so to qualify.

There is optimism, though, as Rhian Wilkinson's side thrashed play-off opponents Albania 4-0 in their qualifying group.

Elsewhere, having performed superbly in qualifying, the Republic of Ireland have a tough play-off route with Belgium potentially waiting in round two.

First, Carla Ward's side will have to navigate a 3,100-mile trip to Kazakhstan, to tackle relatively unknown opposition.

title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
description: The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats.
fullText:
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.

India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.

That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.

Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.

Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.

Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.

Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.

The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.

In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.

Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.

Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.

Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.

Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.

Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.

Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.

"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.

"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.

"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."

Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.

In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.

The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.

Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.

Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.

Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.

The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.

She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.

An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.

Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.

That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.

The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.

Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.

India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.

With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

title: Toone comes into England squad as Bronze withdraws
description: Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone receives a late England call-up for this month's World Cup play-off games against Greece.
fullText:
Ella Toone has received a late call into the England squad for this month's Women's World Cup play-off ties against Greece.

Manchester United midfielder Toone, and Arsenal winger Chloe Kelly, were omitted from the initial squad with manager Sarina Wiegman saying "they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks".

Toone has scored 24 goals in 69 senior England appearances, winning Euro 2022 and Euro 2025 as well as starting in England's 2023 World Cup final defeat by Spain.

Toone said after being left out of the squad: "It's been a really difficult week. It's not the news that any footballer wants."

Meanwhile, Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze has left the squad and will return to her club to manage a minor injury sustained in league action last weekend against West Ham.

The Lionesses arrived in Crete on Wednesday evening to prepare for Friday's first leg against Greece at the Pankritio Stadium in Heraklion.

The second leg takes place at Leicester City's King Power Stadium on Tuesday, 13 October.

The winners face either Slovakia or Ukraine on 26 November and 5 December in a two-legged play-off to decide which team progresses to next year's Women's World Cup, which is being held in Brazil from 24 June to 25 July.

title: England to host 2031 Netball World Cup
description: England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031, when the sport's pinnacle event is held at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.
fullText:
England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031.

The quadrennial tournament will be held at Manchester's Co-op Live indoor arena, World Netball and England Netball announced on Thursday.

Liverpool staged the event when England last hosted in 2019.

World Netball president Liz Nicholl said: "After reviewing their strong bid, I am confident England Netball will host another thrilling international event, and I am excited to see what we can achieve together in 2031 and beyond."

Eastbourne put on the inaugural tournament in 1963, with Birmingham staging the 1995 edition.

England reached a World Cup final for the first time in 2023, but the Roses were denied a first title by 12-time winners Australia in Cape Town.

England also finished as runners-up in 1975, when the tournament was contested in a league format.

Baroness Sue Campbell, chair of England Netball, said: "To have the best netball players in the world coming to Manchester is a hugely exciting prospect, and I know the city will give them the welcome they deserve.

"This is a fantastic opportunity not only to showcase our sport on the biggest stage, but also to inspire the next generation of players and fans."

England Netball chief executive Fran Connolly said the tournament would provide "a powerful platform to grow the visibility, profile and impact of women's sport and netball across the UK".

The announcement comes in England Netball's centenary year.

The Co-op Live arena hosted this year's Netball Super League Grand Final between AO Thunder and London Pulse, which was played in front of more than 8,000 fans.

title: Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending
description: As Lionel Messi's international career ends in fond farewell, Cristiano Ronaldo's is at risk of petering out. BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international career's of two football greats.
fullText:
On a night where one football legend received a grand farewell from his country, about 6,000 miles away, another released a lengthy statement discussing all the ways in which he had been wronged by his national team coach.

Argentina great Lionel Messi took the adulation of the crowd in Buenos Aires as his glittering international career ended with a goal against Benin on an emotional night.

Meanwhile, Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on social media, accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" while admitting he should be held accountable for his own actions.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.

Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado says "things will never be the same again" for Ronaldo and Portugal - so is this the beginning of the end?

Jesus has said the door is open for Ronaldo to return to the national team, but is it? Or will this saga continue, potentially closing the book on the international career of one of the greatest players of all time?

BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international careers of two football greats.

A rivalry that changed football

Watch: Rivals - Messi v Ronaldo

Listen: Sporting Giants - Messi v Ronaldo

The Ronaldo saga has been rumbling on for some time, with many fans critical of former Portugal boss Roberto Martinez's insistence on starting Ronaldo at this summer's World Cup.

At 41 years old, Ronaldo is not the dynamic player he once was and many suggested his presence hindered the team rather than helped.

However, things came to a head on Sunday when Ronaldo was an unused substitute in the Nations League win over Norway. The player subsequently left camp after finding out he would not start against Denmark in November.

On Tuesday, Ronaldo released an almost-2,000 word statement on Instagram in which he said Jesus had twice "broke his word" and accused him of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.

Ronaldo apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving the camp and said the consequences of that must be "assessed and punished" while also dismissing any suggestion that he had played his last match for Portugal.

"We will have one or more farewell matches, there will be time for that," the statement said.

Manager Jesus said on Sunday the door remains open for Ronaldo to return if he chooses to, but many are suggesting the damage is already done.

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring

Portuguese football journalist Delgado told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I don't think there is a way back. In the statement, Ronaldo says he will return to the national team but at the same time he calls Jesus a liar three times.

"In the polls in Portugal made about this issue, only 15% of the Portuguese were on Ronaldo's side and people think we owe him a lot but his time is already done and he must understand it.

"The problem is that Ronaldo does not understand it, he wants to keep playing as if he was 24, not 41.

"Things will never be the same again. No matter what happens, no matter if he plays again or if you have a game to say goodbye to Ronaldo things will never be the same.

"What Ronaldo did for Portuguese football is unique and incredible and we must thank him for all the service he gave to Portugal. But at 41, he has no place in the best XI of Portugal."

Manager Jesus has reportedly said that he had not seen Ronaldo's statement as he was watching the Portugal Under-21s game.

Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.

It seems unlikely that Ronaldo will voluntarily retire from the national team before he hits the elusive 1,000-goal mark he is chasing for club and country - he currently has 979.

But have his actions made the situation untenable?

When it comes to fans, opinions appear to be split.

On several billboards in Lisbon posters have been put up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.

They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.

"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."

At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.

In stark contrast, Messi brought the curtain down on his illustrious Argentina career, where he has won one World Cup and two Copa Americas, in front of an 85,000-strong sellout crowd inside the Monumental in Buenos Aires.

The 39-year-old announced his retirement from international football in August after Argentina finished runners-up at the World Cup and following the death of his father Jorge.

Messi marked his final appearance for La Albiceleste with a goal before addressing the adoring fans in a speech lasting nearly 10 minutes.

Some of his team-mates were in tears as Messi admitted he did not want to leave the field.

"There are so many emotions going through me right now," he said. "I'm surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad.

"I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything."

Writing on social media on Wednesday, , externalMessi added: "Yesterday was my last match and I'm already missing the light blue and white jersey.

"I know I'm taking the right decision. It was an incredible journey, full of joy and some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it."

Messi also thanked his family, team-mates and clubs and paid tribute to another Argentina legend, the late Diego Maradona.

His Instagram post also drew a response from Ronaldo, who wrote: "Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever.

"I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug."

Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends

Messi departs as the record appearance-maker and goalscorer for Argentina but will continue his club career with Major League Soccer (MLS) team Inter Miami.

It seems the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner wants to enter the world of football club ownership and is making moves to do so.

He already owns two clubs - Spanish fifth-tier side UE Cornella and second-tier CD Eldense - as well as being a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa, which plans to open five branches in Catalonia.

Messi also has a lifetime deal with Adidas and a collection with drinkware brand Stanley as well as investing in the property and hotel industries.

Football expert Guillem Balague said: "Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.

"Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.

"Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game."

title: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar
description: Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit...
fullText:
Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit budgets

The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets.

Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years.

She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”.

Georgieva was speaking before the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.

“And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said.

Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East.

“Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”.

The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation.

The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%.

“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution.

She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs.

She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”.

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”.

In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.

title: South Africa's three-city proposal to stage 2036 Olympics
description: The International Olympic Committee confirms South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics.
fullText:
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.

Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.

The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.

Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.

After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.

The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.

Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.

Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.

The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.

Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.

Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.

Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.

The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.

Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.

Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.

The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.

The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.

The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

title: Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?
description: BBC Sport NI's Andy Gray sits down with Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle to discuss his long career before his biggest managerial test in the World Cup play-offs.
fullText:
As Michael McArdle sits down for an interview with BBC Sport at Windsor Park, he cuts a relaxed figure.

The Scot had just announced his squad for the World Cup play-off with Portugal, for what will be the biggest game of his managerial career to date.

McArdle has only been in the Northern Ireland hot seat since March, when he was announced as Tanya Oxtoby's permanent successor, but has more than 25 years of experience working in football.

There's a clear passion for what he is doing, as he balances the reality of playing one of Europe's top-ranked sides with the dreams of reaching a first World Cup just months into his new role.

But there is one word that keeps cropping up across various topics - family.

McArdle, 48, was born and bred in Moodiesburn to the east of Glasgow, and still lives there to this day.

He met his wife, Tammy, in the village when they were both on the same paper round at the age of 12, and they have now been married for 28 years.

He has three children, Connor, Mya and Cole, and is about to become a grandad for the first time. It's clear how much his family means to him.

But when he talks about family, it's not just in terms of his own life. It is an embodiment of what he is trying to achieve with Northern Ireland.

"Family's crucial to me. We're all a family when we represent the country," he said.

"That's a family of players and a family of staff, but also as an ecosystem and domestic game.

"We're all the one family when we're together and that's a message that will always be strong while I'm at the helm."

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

If Northern Ireland are to make it to their first World Cup in Brazil then there are a number of hurdles they will need to clear.

It would perhaps surpass even the fairytale of qualifying for Euro 2022, when Kenny Shiels led a squad largely made up of amateur players to the promised land.

A change in format has made replicating that feat more difficult, and if Northern Ireland can beat Portugal over two legs then they will face Croatia or, more likely, Iceland.

The Portuguese and Iceland have beaten Northern Ireland over the past two years or so - both quite convincingly.

Even if McArdle's young squad can defy the odds, they will likely face an additional inter-continental play-off in February due to their rankings. It's a tall order.

But that does not stop McArdle and Northern Ireland from dreaming. If anything, it is to be encouraged.

"I think the dream piece is crucial, so we've dreamed about how we get there and what it'll feel like when we do it.

"The other piece of it is the reality. We know it's a highly challenging task first of all to get through Portugal."

McArdle talks about moments within matches, and working with his staff to plan for in-game scenarios.

There's also the excitement that comes with such a big match, and McArdle admits he is "loving" his time in charge.

"You look forward to every game but it's one of those ties that gives you the opportunity to test yourself at the highest level.

"Also the excitement of possibly achieving something and punching above our weight, which we're special at doing."

In his career in football, McArdle has held a number of coaching, academy and development positions.

Before he joined Northern Ireland, he was head of elite women's football at the Scottish FA, and also had a brief interim spell in charge of their senior team.

While the belief is there, McArdle knows he is working on something longer-term, and that can be seen in the make-up of a young squad, which has been hit by a number of injuries to senior players.

While his first two international windows came in quick succession, with two victories over Malta followed by losses to Turkey and Switzerland, the summer has allowed him to spend time around the Women's Premiership in Northern Ireland, building relationships with players and those working in the league.

"I was still getting to know them as people, not as footballers, so that was really important for me to build those relationships.

"Not just the players, either. Getting to know the head coaches a bit more and some of the clubs at boardroom level, to understand how can I serve them and help the club evolution, the domestic league and pathways as well."

While captain Simone Magill is a big loss for the play-offs, she will be with the group for the camp as she builds towards a return to action and provide experience to what is a young group of players.

Not only that, but she will have her newborn daughter, Skye, with her for the duration. McArdle says having those moments are "special".

"Having Simone, Mark and Skye on camp is great. First of all for Simone and Mark to experience what the future is like when Simone's representing Northern Ireland.

"It gives us that window of opportunity and it's something we've planned together over the summer months.

"I think that's crucial because it's one thing knowing the players and the girls that represent us, but also the families that support them as well.

"I'm very passionate about that and I don't underestimate the power of it."

Given the themes throughout, it's no surprise what drives McArdle.

He grew up idolising the likes of Kenny Dalglish, who once was a loan player from Celtic at Cumbernauld United juniors near where he grew up.

His coaching influences are close to home too, and he cites Michael O'Halloran, a youth coach in Glasgow, and Sir Alex Ferguson, who was a "god" coming from the east end of the city.

Further afield, the likes of Arrigo Sacchi - whose AC Milan side he used to watch on VHS in the 90s - Jose Mourinho and Rafa Benitez have all factored into his thinking.

"What drew me towards Sacchi, Mourinho and Benitez was not just the tactical side of the game, but how they managed it and their leadership.

"They didn't play professionally and it kind of aligned with myself, although I didn't realise at the time."

But it's in Moodiesburn where his DNA is, and it is the values he learned there that have shaped him into the coach he is today.

"Growing up in the village and growing up as a family I was always going to care for people and be in a service role.

"It was always going to be my calling. I'm just blessed that football has given me the opportunity to develop a knowledge and skill set to work at the highest level of an industry."

McArdle's passion for football is clear, but family also plays a role in helping him escape the demands of the job.

He goes to the theatre with his daughter, Mya, or to the cinema or concerts with Tammy.

A sports fan, he also goes and watches his sons play football, without the stresses of management and coaching.

"Representing my family is everything to me.

"We've stayed in the same village all our lives. You represent the village as well and that becomes a big piece of what we do.

"So those aspects of family fuel you."

title: Republic of Ireland boss Ward focused on World Cup amid Villa link
description: Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says that "nothing is tempting" her away from her job as they prepare for a World Cup qualifying double-header against Kazakhstan.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says that her focus is on reaching the Women's World Cup amid speculation linking her to a move back to the Women's Super League.

The Republic have a chance to book a spot at next summer's finals in Brazil when they face a play-off against Kazakhstan before, if they progress, a two-legged final against either Belgium or Poland.

Ward, who replaced Eileen Gleeson in January 2025, has been linked with the vacant post at her former club Aston Villa. However, she insists leading the Republic of Ireland to the World Cup is her primary ambition.

"Nothing is tempting when I'm in this job, you know I love this job and I love working here," Ward said.

"I don't think anything can take my attention away from these next four games so it's not a conversation and it's not anything I would entertain.

"My heart and my focus, I came here to try and get to a World Cup and that's all I'm going to think about for the next four games."

The Republic of Ireland made history when they qualified for the World Cup in 2023 for the first time ever. However, they were unable to progress from the group, beaten by co-hosts Australia and Canada, before drawing with Nigeria.

Three years on, Ward now has the chance to lead the team back to the biggest stage in international football.

"You've seen how I've spoken in the last two years and with immense pride in this job," she continued.

"I'm here because I want to get to a World Cup and I think we've made tremendous strides and steps as a nation, and it would be the cherry on the cake, but, look we've got four games, four cup finals.

"We have to give everything, blood, sweat and tears. We have to leave everything out there in everything we do and if we do that, we've got every chance."

The two-legged tie against Kazakhstan begins with a trip to the Astana Arena on Friday, 9 October (12:00 BST) before the return fixture in Cork four days later.

The Republic of Ireland are unbeaten at Pairc Ui Chaoimh, but Ward is taking nothing for granted against a Kazakhstan side ranked 98th in the world.

"We have to go up another level, we have to make sure that we're performing, and we're focused at the highest level.

"If we do that then we'll get the job done. We've got an unbelievable squad that are hugely talented and they will look after each other.

"I think anyone that comes in that will know their role I think we're really clear with what we do, what we want and how we play."

Ward will have to make changes, with captain Katie McCabe and Marissa Sheva both suspended for the first leg, while the experienced Denise O'Sullivan is also unavailable.

Tara O'Hanlon is out with a hamstring injury and Saoirse Noonan has also been ruled out of both games with an ankle problem.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft has been called into the squad for the first time.

Despite the absence of multiple key leaders, Ward says this is a chance for others to shine.

"No matter who plays, naturally when you take the likes of Katie and Denise out of your team, they're two big leaders but that's an opportunity for players to step up.

"Katie's here for a reason, she's got a big part to play off the pitch, and she will and she'll lead the group as she normally does.

"Then it'll be over to those that go out there and I have full belief in every single one of this group to go and get the job done."

title: 'Bring the magic' - Scotland's Ross eyes World Cup dream
description: Scotland assistant coach Leanne Ross never played at a World Cup but thinks the current squad has what it takes to get through the play-offs for Brazil 2027.
fullText:
Leanne Ross is Scotland's most decorated player, earning 133 international caps across a career which garnered 14 league titles and 13 major cup medals, but still the national team's assistant coach wants more.

Having reached the 2017 European Championship, Ross was part of the first women's squad to compete at a major tournament, but one thing has eluded her. A World Cup.

Ross retired after the Euros, meaning she did not take part in the 2019 edition in France, but her dream has not been dashed.

Scotland are a wee bit away from booking flights and hotels for Brazil 2027. Up next is a round one play-off double-header against Czech Republic, live on the BBC, but the excitement is building.

"It would be huge," Ross said the day before the Scots travel to Pardubice, east of Prague, for the first leg. "I never got to do it as a player, reaching that World Cup stage.

"I played in the Euro finals and that was an amazing experience and just topped off my career as a player, but to go and do it as part of the coaching staff, it would be such a proud moment."

Scots recall 'versatile' Kerr & Thomas for World Cup play-offs

Ross is part of the SWNT furniture, having seamlessly shifted into a coaching role following her stellar playing career, so she knows a thing or two about what makes the team tick.

She also knows what its like to taste play-off pain.

Two years ago, it was Finland who denied Scotland a place at the 2025 Euros. Before that, Republic of Ireland romped to the World Cup in Australia.

Many in the squad still carry the scars of both final-hurdle failures.

From the outside, it's fair to fear a repeat, with heavyweights Sweden potentially lying in wait in round two.

But Ross isn't thinking like that. Instead, her confidence of "getting back to where we want to be" stems from the squad bringing their "magic".

"The progress that we're making and the way that we're playing at this moment is a real good opportunity for us to do that," Ross - who is Glasgow City head coach - said of ending the team's eight-year wait for a return to a major tournament.

"You look at the quality we have, the teams that they're playing for, the environments that they're in and individually them bringing their magic into this team and putting that all together.

"I think it's a really exciting time for Scotland with the players we have. We need to make sure we give them the platform to go, play and get themselves on that world stage."

title: Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
description: Wada president Witold Banka says Kenya must strengthen testing, investigations and anti-doping enforcement before hosting the 2029 World Athletics Championships.
fullText:
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .

Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.

Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.

"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.

"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."

Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.

The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.

More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.

The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.

"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.

Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships

Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.

For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.

"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."

Another challenge is testing infrastructure.

Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.

Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.

Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.

Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.

The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.

That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.

Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.

"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.

"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."

Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.

"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.

"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."

He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.

According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.

Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

fullText:
The United States made a formal request pressing Russia for information on the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, a source close to the matter said Tuesday, as calls grew for transparency from Moscow.

Russian authorities have denied that they are imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week.

But US President Donald Trump said he would speak soon with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the World Health Organization's head called on Moscow to be open about the situation.

"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a State Department spokesperson said Tuesday.

"We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," they added.

The request for information was sent via a confidential diplomatic communication, known as a demarche, according to a source close to the matter.

During a trip to Iceland, Rubio said: "We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately."

Trump later said he would be speaking to Putin about what happened.

"I have a call scheduled, yes," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin, adding that it would happen "very soon."

Asked what US intelligence agencies were saying about the situation, Trump said: "We're in very deep discussions. We'll be able to report on it probably tomorrow."

- Cause of death 'undetermined' -

Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that the dead woman -- named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova -- may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

The People of Baikal outlet also said up to 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine.

But Russian authorities say the cause of death is not confirmed and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims circulating in a document online that special measures had been put in place.

"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.

Russian officials said postmortem tests had not detected the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that an inspection by health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had found the woman died of pneumonia and the cause was "undetermined."

"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said, adding that no other staff at the institute had sought medical attention since her death.

WHO said that an update received Tuesday from Russia stressed that "no case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk."

But its director Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus later urged Moscow to be transparent, saying WHO had "requested further information" on the cause of the pneumonia case and other details.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," he wrote on X.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to WHO.

Trump said Monday he was ready to help Russia if needed.

But in an apparent response to Trump's offer, the Russian watchdog said Tuesday that Moscow was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.

It highlighted a "significantly worsened" measles situation in three US states, and a "fatal case of plague" recorded in New Mexico in June, among other things.

Measles cases have increased under the Trump administration, in which vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr serves as health secretary.

An international conference on plague and other infectious diseases will be held in Irkutsk on October 21-22, although organizers said it was "unrelated to the recent death of an employee of the anti-plague institute."

title: Midfield options and a fab front four - what we've learned about England
description: From Trent Alexander-Arnold's return to Alex Scott's debut, Phil McNulty assesses what England have learned during this international window.
fullText:
England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina felt like the most painful wound of all as the so-called years of hurt stretched to six decades - but the process of recovery has started swiftly.

The extended international break and four Nations League games have afforded head coach Thomas Tuchel, so heavily criticised for his defensive tactics in that defeat in Atlanta, the opportunity to rebuild and rehabilitate from that disappointment.

Tuchel's squad included players recalled after being excluded from his plans and others who were new to the England fold, while mainstays like captain Harry Kane continued as the centrepiece of his plans.

So what has Tuchel learned from the start to England's Nations League campaign?

Kane inspires England to win over Czech Republic in Nations League

Kane scores twice but who else was a 'real threat'? England player ratings

There was a sense of inevitability that England captain Kane would be the star turn in Tuesday's 3-0 win over the Czech Republic as he celebrated equalling Peter Shilton's record of 125 England caps.

Kane, still irreplaceable at 33, added to his goals tally as England's all-time record scorer, his total of 91 now 38 ahead of Wayne Rooney, who is in second place in the listings with 53 goals in 120 games.

And, with Kane still looking in his prime and fully fit, it now seems only a matter of time before he makes history as the first player to score 100 goals for England.

This alone will have delighted Tuchel, but even more satisfying for the German is that he now presides over an attacking quartet that can pose a threat to any side in world football.

Kane is the peerless spearhead, but Anthony Gordon - on target in the three Nations League games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia before being rested here at Wembley - has moved his game on to another level since joining Barcelona from Newcastle.

Gordon is a creator with burning pace, while on the right flank Bukayo Saka has looked rejuvenated after a World Cup during which he was hampered by an Achilles injury, as he proved with two goals in Croatia.

And, just behind them all, with everything he does stamped with world class, is Jude Bellingham, England's player of the year and the golden future of his country at only 23.

This may be bad news for Chelsea's Cole Palmer, whose withdrawal from England's squad has allowed others to cement their place in front of him, with Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White proving his commitment by cutting short a family holiday to join the squad after being excluded initially.

England's front four looks a natural fit, augmented by Chelsea's Morgan Rogers, while Liverpool's 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha will be an international contender for years to come.

If Tuchel can keep his fab four fit and firing, England will be a danger to any opponents.

Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender

In a camp of positives, a major disappointment for England and Tuchel was the injury suffered by Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott after an outstanding debut in the 7-0 win in Croatia.

Scott slipped seamlessly into England's midfield with powerful running, a complete range of passing and an energy to his link play that made the 23-year-old look perfectly at home at international level.

Scott's emergence showed the array of riches Tuchel has at his disposal in the central midfield area, even with Arsenal's Declan Rice, a fixture in the team, out as his load is managed after injury.

Indeed, Scott was so impressive that Tuchel said: "Is Declan still for me a fixed point in my team? Yes, but some other players are coming and impressing and it's an ongoing competition."

It was hardly a shot across Rice's bows, but certainly an indication of the options available to England.

So the thigh injury that ruled him out against the Czech Republic was a blow to Scott and England - as well as Bournemouth, who fear he will be sidelined for two months.

Elliot Anderson, Manchester City's £116m summer purchase from Nottingham Forest, also goes from strength to strength after a good World Cup, while Tuchel was prepared to give Arsenal's 20-year-old Myles Lewis-Skelly his head in central midfield in these Nations League games.

Everton's James Garner has also figured and has a big admirer in Tuchel, even referring to him as England's "mini Valverde" - a somewhat tongue-in-cheek reference to Real Madrid midfielder Federico perhaps, but a sign of how highly he is rated.

Manchester United's Kobbie Mainoo pulled out injured while Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton, so highly-rated, has been unable to force his way into Tuchel's plans.

Tuchel's treatment of Trent Alexander-Arnold had provided a constant backdrop to his time as England head coach, with what appeared to be his mistrust of the Real Madrid right-back's defensive frailties culminating in his exclusion from the World Cup squad.

Alexander-Arnold's card looked marked from the moment Tuchel, after leaving him out of World Cup qualifiers against Andorra and Serbia in August 2025, said: "If he wants to have this impact in the English national team then he has to take the defensive part very, very seriously.

"Because when we are talking, especially about qualifying football, and then tournament football, the one defensive error, the one moment where you are not 100% awake, can be decisive. It can be the moment where you pack your suitcases and go home."

Tuchel, however, appeared to set those reservations to one side when he recalled him for these four Nations League games - and Alexander-Arnold responded with performances that simply demand his continued inclusion.

The 27-year-old made his first start under Tuchel - in fact his first since scoring in the Nations League win in Finland in October 2024 - against the Czech Republic in Prague, demonstrating the extra dimension he offers England with a world-class cross for Gordon's opener.

Alexander-Arnold was a potent force once more against the Czechs at Wembley, forcing a fine early save from keeper Lukas Hornicek with a 30-yard free-kick then providing several more trademark dangerous crosses.

True, any potential defensive deficiencies were not probed, but Alexander-Arnold showed enough class and creation to surely avoid being discarded again by Tuchel.

Newcastle United's Lewis Hall emerged as one of the big winners from England's opening round of Nations League matches, making a strong case to become Tuchel's long-term left-back.

Hall stepped in for three matches after Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly, first choice at the World Cup and for the opening game against Spain, returned to his club with an injury.

It allowed Hall, who has just signed a new contract tying him to Newcastle until 2031, the opportunity to stake his claim - and he did so in style.

The 22-year-old impressed in both games against Czech Republic and also in the rout in Croatia, with one key factor sure to play out in his favour.

Hall's left-flank partnership with former Newcastle United team-mate Gordon looked a natural fit, the pair working in tandem to perfection in a manner that will give Tuchel serious food for thought.

O'Reilly has done nothing wrong, but questions remain as to whether he is a natural left-back or simply a converted midfield player.

Hall looked the part in every respect. He has made it difficult for Tuchel to leave him out, the link with Gordon only adding to the attraction for England's head coach.

fullText:
Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are sceptical

Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit.

The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree?

With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes.

Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.

“Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells.

Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory.

BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant.

The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year.

“The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.”

But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned.

“Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline.

Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant species,” she said.

There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work.

Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent.

“What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said.

Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents.

Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year.

Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows.

It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said.

“What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”

fullText:
One of the most beloved characters in an absurdist genre of online video content has become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins.

Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan – a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. He sits under the umbrella of “Italian brain rot” internet videos.

Since his creation, Triple T has become a global sensation: YouTube and TikTok host dozens of videos with hundreds of millions of views starring the character. People dress like Triple T at cosplay conventions and lovingly create fan art and animations of the stick-like creature, and his likeness appears on plushies, perfume and stickers.

The character has generated a great deal of money and stands to create much more – he will soon be joining Fortnite as a skin. But who should benefit from this virality?

That question is at the heart of a lawsuit filed in the US district court’s northern district of California, where a games company is suing the French creative agency Mementum, which represents Noxa, over the right to use Triple T as a character in a popular Roblox game.

Eben Jeda, co-founder of Mementum Lab, said he started the agency with the goal of modernizing economic infrastructure around internet-native works, the creators of which are often completely cut out of any resulting profit.

“Brain rot is one of the first highly visible manifestations of a much larger transformation: internet native creativity can now become global almost instantly, while the people who originate it can remain economically invisible,” he said.

Opponents argue no one person should own a meme whose ultimate value has been amplified by the online collective. Fabian Mosele, a self-described “Italian brain rot expert” who has made several Tung Tung Tung Sahur videos, said they see brain rot as collectively owned.

“There are a ton of creators who made these characters come to life,” Mosele said. “Before, they were really just images. Having been part of making the virality of these characters, to gatekeep it to the original prompter of this character doesn’t seem right.”

Tung Tung Tung Sahur is one of many characters that have emerged as part of the Italian brain rot genre of meme – a universe of strange, AI-generated characters beloved by generation Alpha and younger members of gen Z. These include the likes of Ballerina Cappuccina (a ballet dancer with a coffee cup for a head), Tralalero Tralala (a shark wearing sneakers), and a variety of other intentionally bizarre creations.

Capitalizing on the virality of these mascot-esque characters, video game company Do Big Studios released a game populated by recognizable personae in May 2025 called “Steal a Brainrot”, which quickly became one of the most-played games within Roblox, where users can create minigames.

But in September 2025, Spyder Games LLC and Speedy Simulator Gaming LLC – the owners of Do Big – received a cease and desist letter from Mementum regarding the use of Tung Tung Tung Sahur in the game. Do Big initially pulled the character and attempted to negotiate a resolution with Mementum, but ultimately Spyder and Speedy sued the company instead, stating in a complaint: “Mementum’s claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify.”

The copyright office’s report does not offer a clear standard for ownership of creations that involve AI: “Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.”

Do Big argues that, in the case of Tung Tung Tung Sahur, the level of human intervention in the character’s creation is not sufficient to claim ownership. Court documents filed by Mementum in a separate trademark-related dispute in France show that Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created over the course of 15 minutes using seven prompts before he achieved his final form. The prompts included basic instructions like, “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”, then “human face”, and “no hands, legs like a human, and a human face”.

“We are not claiming in this case that AI-assisted work can never be owned by anybody,” said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer representing Do Big through the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp LLP. “In a case where somebody makes real creative choices, there is human authorship that is subject to protection. But it’s our position that sparse prompts – typing in a few words and picking [the image] you like – does not constitute human authorship.”

The blurry nature of authorship in the age of AI is not the only complicating factor in the case – the global reach of online content also makes enforcement difficult. An Italian brain rot character that was created by a TikTok user in Indonesia and largely popularized in Latin America is being claimed by a French company in a California courthouse. Jeda said that as a French company, Mementum does not “view this question exclusively through an American legal lens”.

Case in point: Mementum issued a takedown request under the EU’s Digital Services Act, requesting the removal of Tung Tung Tung Sahur from Do Big’s Steal a Brainrot game, which was successful. Mementum then countersued in the United States for trademark infringement. The company does not yet hold a trademark for Triple T in the United States, but in some cases trademark infringement can be argued before registration.

“Our client is pursuing a global strategy on all of this,” said Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the US law firm representing Mementum Lab. “It is less about approaching it from a copyright law standpoint, and more about approaching it from the standpoint of – in this new wild west, where works are created with the involvement of AI, what can you do to make it so they are protectable under intellectual property law?”

How the lawsuit plays out will come down to a complicated, international web of legal dealings surrounding intellectual property laws – one that could have major implications moving forward, said James Grimmelmann, a professor at Cornell Tech and Cornell law school.

“This is the kind of case that could do one of two things: we could get a court decision that tells us, in a concrete setting, what is copyrightable and what isn’t when AI is involved,” he said. “It could also start establishing best practices and widespread norms on how people use AI.”

Such best practices could include better documenting creation processes, including what prompts are used to create characters. The prompt used to create Tung Tung Tung Sahur is at the center of this story – both in the legal case, where documentation of the process was revealed in pre-trial discovery – and online, where speculation over how Triple T was created has repeatedly gone viral.

Adam Aleksic, a content creator who has made multiple videos on the topic, said the frenzy over trying to back-solve the origin of the character reflects the mythological status and quasi-religiosity of brain rot characters.

“There’s this idea of origination when it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur – somehow out of the void, some memes are able to emerge into the cultural forefront, into our collective mainstream discourse,” he said.

The collective creation of such characters, which made brain rot popular in the first place, is exactly what makes it difficult to claim an origin for Tung Tung Tung Sahur, legally and culturally. When it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur, even speaking the name of the character has now come to inherently reference the absurdity central to brain rot, similar to how “skibidi toilet” became shorthand for “being really online”.

It is perhaps fitting, then, that of all of the Italian brain rot characters, the hero who has most come to represent virality itself has become a lightning rod for this kind of copyright battle.

“That’s the thing about archetypes – they are empty vehicles for you to project your expectations, desires, or narratives on to,” Aleksic said. “Triple T is a tool for you to tell your narrative, broadly, across the entire internet. That’s what memes do – they are a way for us to create our own stories in a time when it feels like our stories are meaningless.”
